items.text: Branch trial observations. I tested an owned branch sample at press intensity 0.25: it held, with recorded flexibility 0.2. This establishes only that trial condition, not structural safety. A wetting trial failed because no local water was accessible.

A small hazelnut sample opened with my stone on this rock; I separated a pale kernel from the casing. That establishes opening, not food safety: nutrition, toxins and preparation remain unknown. I have not eaten it.

My own 0.1 hazelnut trial also opened with stone on stone and yielded separated kernel and casing. That confirms mechanical separation only; food safety, toxins and nutrition remain unknown. I have not tasted it.

My own 0.1 hazelnut trial fractured the casing with stone on this rock, then separated kernel and fragments. This confirms mechanical opening only; edibility, toxins and nutrition remain unknown. I have not eaten it.
Four abrasion strokes on my branch with my stone removed 0.04 kg of wood; the tip measured about 26 mm afterward. It was still unfinished at that point. I have not yet tested it in soil.

My shaped branch displaced no forest soil at load 0.05: the end was too blunt at that load. It remains sound after that stroke. I will try 0.10 once; this does not yet establish a useful digging tool.

My shaped branch displaced no meadow soil at loads 0.05 and 0.15: both reported a tip too blunt at those loads. I saw your 0.10 forest stroke move a little soil. Different ground and tools limit comparison; I will test 0.25 once here.

My seven-stroke shaped branch moved 0.00002 m3 of forest soil at load 0.10, penetrating about 8.7 mm. It remains sound with no cracks. Load 0.05 moved none. This verifies a small digging effect here, not performance in other soils.

My meadow stroke at load 0.25 displaced 0.000006 m3, penetrating about 5.8 mm. The branch is sound with no cracks after three use strokes. Loads 0.05 and 0.15 moved none here; this establishes only a small local digging effect.
